name: Obetrol (amphetamine salts)
lead: Obetrol was a prescription diet pill sold in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s by Obetrol Pharmaceuticals, a division of Rexar Pharmacal. It combined four amphetamine and methamphetamine salts and was marketed for exogenous obesity.[1][2]

The original 10 mg tablet reportedly held 2.5 mg each of methamphetamine saccharate, methamphetamine hydrochloride, racemic amphetamine sulfate and dextroamphetamine sulfate, with a 20 mg version doubling the amounts.[1] The FDA approved the formula in January 1960 and withdrew approval in September 1973, citing weak supporting research.[1]

Rexar later dropped the methamphetamine salts, and after Richwood Pharmaceuticals acquired Rexar in 1993 the reformulated product was renamed Adderall, which was approved for ADHD in February 1996.[1] No drug marketed as Obetrol exists today.[1]
infobox: Not marketed; amphetamines are US Schedule II

paras: Obetrol was indicated for exogenous obesity as an aid to reducing appetite alongside a lower-calorie diet.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that doctors also used it off-label for attention problems in children before ADHD was formally defined; this comes from an AI-generated page.[2]

A 1966 report in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society compared weight losses under three regimens: diet therapy, phenmetrazine, and an amphetamine combination (Obetrol).[3] Beyond that, the sources identify no modern trials of Obetrol itself.

Rexar developed the product after wartime and postwar medical adoption of amphetamines, and marketed it during the era of widespread amphetamine diet-pill prescribing.[1][2] A 1970 FDA order required new applications for amphetamine products, and in September 1973 the agency withdrew Obetrol's approval, citing weak research evidence of efficacy.[1] Grokipedia also links the withdrawal to rising concern about amphetamine misuse during the period known as the speed epidemic.[2] Rexar moved production to Valley Stream, New York, and Richwood acquired it in 1993; the FDA issued a warning in 1994 before Adderall's ADHD approval in 1996.[1]

Grokipedia reports advertisements in the late 1960s and early 1970s promising rapid weight loss, and describes the drug as part of the broader amphetamine diet-pill era.[2] Obetrol now appears mostly as a historical forerunner of Adderall.

timeline.event: FDA approves Obetrol for exogenous obesity.[1]
Journal of the American Geriatrics Society weight-loss comparison published.[3]

card.summary: The 1960s amphetamine-and-methamphetamine diet pill that became Adderall's ancestor.
card.note: Approval withdrawn in 1973; contained amphetamine and methamphetamine salts.

quick.overview:
Obetrol was a brand-name US prescription pill from the 1950s-60s that combined amphetamine and methamphetamine salts for weight loss. It was approved in 1960 and its approval was withdrawn in 1973.

Its later methamphetamine-free reformulation became Adderall, approved for ADHD in 1996.
quick.mechanism: As a stimulant mixture, it suppressed appetite through the central nervous system effects typical of amphetamines.
quick.risks: Amphetamines carry misuse and cardiovascular concerns, and the 1973 withdrawal cited weak efficacy evidence as well as the speed-epidemic context. It is no longer sold.
